e.t: Abraamitis, also rendered Avraamitis, is a proper name used to identify a particular person or designation rather than describe a general quality or action. Its meaning is therefore primarily its name-reference, not an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 18:20. The available lexical definition gives no broader sense beyond the names Abraamitis and Avraamitis.

Agaraios; Agareos is a proper name identifying a particular named subject, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. It appears once in the Greek Septuagint, at 1 Chronicles 5:20. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, the specific person or group identified there cannot be described more precisely. The name should therefore be understood as a designation, with its exact reference determined by the context of that passage.

“Hallow” is a verb for making something holy, setting it apart for God, or treating it as sacred. In the LXX corpus, this word is used broadly rather than rarely: it occurs 180 times, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees. Its repeated use in Leviticus, Exodus, and Numbers places it in language about holiness and dedication, though its precise force depends on what is being hallowed in each passage.

Azania is a proper name, referring to a person named Azania. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:10. The available information identifies the name clearly, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain anything further about Azania’s role in that passage.

This LXX verb means to “hold guiltless”—to regard or treat a person as not guilty. It describes an action taken toward someone, rather than simply naming a condition of innocence. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including Judges, Samuel, Kings, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains withholding a charge of guilt or declaring someone free from guilt.

Akous, also rendered Akus, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person by name in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at Ezra 2:61. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific identity and role must be understood from that passage. The name itself carries no further meaning beyond identifying the person named Akous or Akus.

This Greek LXX noun means “hearing,” referring to the act or experience of receiving sound or spoken words. It can describe hearing as a human faculty or the reception of something communicated. Within the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, and Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the act of listening, the ability to hear, or what has been heard.

Aliphaleth is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is also rendered Alifaleth, giving two approved forms of the same personal designation. It occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, in 2 Samuel 23:34. Because this word functions as a name, its basic meaning is the identification of the individual who bears it, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific historical context.

This word means “lamb,” referring to a young sheep. It is a noun used for the animal itself, including lambs presented among offerings and lambs counted as part of a flock or household’s possessions. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 24 times across 24 verses, with many occurrences in Numbers and several in Genesis. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its larger context.

This Greek LXX verb means “remind” or “recall”: it describes bringing something back to a person’s mind or calling it to remembrance. As a verb, it expresses an action—someone causes another person to remember, or a person recalls something previously known. It occurs 22 times in the Greek LXX, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used in varied settings rather than referring to one narrow event.

This adjective means “unfailing”: something dependable that does not fail or give out. It describes a quality of steady reliability rather than a separate action or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in the book of Wisdom, in Wisdom 7:14 and 8:18. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what it describes in each passage, but its basic sense remains consistent: it points to what can be relied on without failing.

This Greek LXX verb means to deem someone or something worthy, or to consider it worthwhile. It expresses an evaluation of value, suitability, or deservingness rather than merely noticing something. In its 36 occurrences in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it can describe regarding a person or matter as worthy of attention, honor, or a particular response. The precise force in any verse depends on what is being evaluated and the surrounding sentence.

d: not diawn hither and thither; not distracted

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something that is not drawn in different directions and is not distracted. It presents steadiness rather than mental or practical scattering: attention, purpose, or movement remains undivided. The word’s stated meaning is “not diawn hither and thither; not distracted.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

“Breathe forth” means to exhale or send breath outward. This Greek LXX verb describes the act of breathing out, focusing on breath leaving a person or creature. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 15:18. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wording, but its central meaning remains the outward release of breath.

This adjective describes something that is not anticipated or has not been looked for—something surprising or unforeseen. It can describe an event, circumstance, or outcome that arrives outside normal expectation. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs four times: once in Wisdom and three times in 3 Maccabees. Its central meaning remains consistent across these occurrences: what happens or appears unexpectedly, rather than what was predicted, prepared for, or expected.

Armenia is a proper name for a place called Armenia. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 37:38. Its meaning is straightforward: it identifies Armenia rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. Because the available information gives only the place-name and reference, the surrounding verse is needed to explain how Armenia functions in that specific passage.

Arsaios, also rendered Arseos, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, in Esther 9:9. The lexical definition identifies the name as “Arsaios; Arseos,” while no English rendering is recorded. Because this is a proper name, its main function is to identify a particular person; its precise significance in Esther depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Asipha (also rendered Asifa) is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament text rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or group by name, but the available information does not establish more about the bearer. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:46. Its precise identity must be read from that passage’s surrounding text.

Atita is a proper name, identifying a person or family group in the Greek Old Testament. It appears twice, once in Ezra 2:42 and once in Nehemiah 7:45, and is rendered consistently as “Atita.” The available word-level information establishes the name itself but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain who Atita was or what role the person or group had in those passages.

This verb means “obscure” or “hide”—to make something unclear, concealed, or no longer visible. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe the act of covering something from view or causing it to disappear from notice. The word occurs 86 times in the Septuagint corpus, across books such as Exodus, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Esther, and Proverbs. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being hidden and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “fearlessness”: the condition of being unafraid or without fear. It names a quality rather than an action, describing a person’s lack of fear. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 15:16. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its comparison, but the word itself points plainly to boldness or freedom from fear. It should therefore be understood as a description of inner courage, not as a separate event or command.

Achiab, also rendered Akhiav, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Jeremiah 36:21–22. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning is the identification of a particular person, not a general idea that can be defined like a common noun or verb. The name’s precise referent and significance in either verse must be determined from the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Achiou, also rendered Akhiu, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 26:7. Because it is a proper name, its main function is to identify a particular person; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to say more about that individual. The name itself does not provide a broader meaning beyond identifying the person who bears it.

This word is a proper name, represented by the forms “Baithegeneth” and “Vetheyeneth.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general object; it identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The word occurs once, in Joshua 19:27, so its ordinary meaning is limited to this name rather than a broader recurring concept. The exact nature of the named entity must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

Belgai, also rendered Velye, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:9. Because this is a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it distinguishes the person named in that passage. The exact significance of the individual depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word means “cluster,” referring to several fruits or similar objects gathered together. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament to describe a grouped bunch, especially in passages involving grapes and their fruit. The word occurs 13 times across 11 verses in the Greek Old Testament, including references in Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Song of Songs. Its central idea remains a connected group rather than a single item, while the surrounding passage identifies what has been gathered into the cluster.

This Greek LXX noun means “skin stripped off; hide,” referring to the outer covering removed from an animal or body. It names a physical material rather than an action or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing in Leviticus and Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: animal skin or hide that has been stripped off.

Gamōl, also rendered Gamol, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person or place named Gamol in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 31:23. Because no further lexical definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the name should be understood primarily as a proper designation, with its precise referent determined by the passage in which it appears.

This word is a proper name rendered “Geththa” or “Yeththa.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 5:8. Because the available wording gives only the name itself and no verse text or surrounding context, its specific referent cannot be explained further here. The two approved renderings indicate how the same name may appear in English, while its basic function remains that of a proper name.

This word means “giant,” referring to a person understood as exceptionally large or formidable. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for giants as a recognizable group or individual description. The word occurs 40 times in the LXX, appearing across books such as Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a giant or giants.

This LXX noun is associated with “Debratha” and “stretch.” The first wording functions as a name, while “stretch” gives the ordinary lexical sense recorded for the word. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 5:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise role in that occurrence cannot be described further without adding unsupported context. This noun means “marking off by lines,” referring to the act of setting something apart or defining it through drawn lines. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 43:12. The word’s central idea is clear from its definition: boundaries or divisions are established by marking lines. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “shew through” or “let.” It describes an action of allowing something to pass through or become apparent, depending on the sentence. It occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Wisdom 17:6. Because the word appears only there and no verse text is provided, its precise force in that passage cannot be explained further from the word alone. Its basic sense remains an active verb expressing showing through or allowing.

This verb means “transmit the sound of”—to cause a sound or message to carry outward so that it can be heard. It describes the spreading or passing on of sound rather than merely making a sound. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning concerns sound being conveyed from one place or person to others.

This verb means to pursue someone or drive someone out. It describes active movement against a person—chasing them, forcing them away, or expelling them. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Lamentations 5:5, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its basic sense remains clear: someone is being pursued or driven away rather than peacefully departing. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain which aspect is intended there.

This noun means “service,” referring to the act or duty of serving. It identifies service itself rather than the person who serves or the command to serve. In the Greek Old Testament and one deuterocanonical occurrence, it appears 43 times, showing that it is a recurring term for service across these writings. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “ill-affected,” describing someone who is negatively or unfavorably disposed toward another person or matter. It points to an adverse attitude rather than a neutral or favorable one. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Esther and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a disposition marked by ill will or unfavorable feeling.

This Greek LXX verb means to “enclose in a collar,” describing the act of surrounding or fastening something with a collar. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Proverbs 6:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the act of enclosing something in a collar.

This Greek LXX verb means “accustomed,” describing what someone is used to doing or what regularly happens. It points to a settled habit or customary practice rather than a single unusual action. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Numbers, Sirach, 4 Maccabees, and Susanna. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is familiarity formed through repeated practice.

Eliana is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 8:4, and its meaning is presented simply as “Eliana.” Because it functions as a proper name, its main purpose is to identify the person named in the passage. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s role or significance there.

This Greek LXX noun means “merchant”—a person engaged in buying and selling goods. It refers to people involved in commerce and trade, including those who travel or deal in goods from different places. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, with especially frequent use in Ezekiel. Its basic sense remains focused on a trader or commercial dealer; the surrounding passage determines what goods, people, or trading activity are in view.

This verb means “make oneself a nest on”—to settle or build a nest upon something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:16. Its basic sense is clear, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what is being nested on and how the image functions there.

This Greek LXX verb means “ride away.” It describes the action of departing while riding, rather than simply moving on foot. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Habakkuk 1:8, so its precise force there belongs to that passage’s surrounding context. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: someone rides away or departs on horseback or another riding animal. The word expresses movement away from a place or situation through riding.

This Greek LXX verb means “keep the festival”: to observe a festival or appointed celebration. It describes an action, calling people to mark a sacred occasion rather than merely mentioning the festival itself. The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 15 verses, from Exodus through Zechariah. Its use in laws and festival passages gives it a practical sense: faithfully observing the designated celebration. The exact significance of a particular occurrence depends on the surrounding passage, but the word consistently points to celebrating or observing a festival.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “recognition”—the act of recognizing or acknowledging something or someone. It names a form of knowing that brings something into view as recognized, rather than describing an action or command. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including three occurrences in Hosea, and also appears once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains recognition or acknowledgment.

This verb means to “march against,” describing an advance directed toward an opposing person or force. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs six times across Isaiah, Zechariah, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic emphasis is not simply movement, but movement in opposition—going out against someone or something. The precise force of the action in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to an opposing advance.

This noun means “concession” or “permission”: the granting of allowance for something to happen. It describes authorization rather than an action, person, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 3:7. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what was permitted there, but the word itself points to consent or allowance being given. Its central idea is that someone grants room or approval for an action.

Esēl, also rendered Esil, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament translation of 1 Chronicles. The name occurs six times in four verses, all within 1 Chronicles 8–9, where genealogical lists preserve personal names. The available information establishes the name’s identity and use, but does not provide an expanded meaning or interpretation for the name itself. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding genealogy and verse context.

This word means “inner,” referring to what is inside or toward the interior. It can describe an inner place or position and may function in a sentence as an adjective, adverb, or preposition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 36 times, with especially frequent use in Ezekiel. Its central idea remains the distinction between what is within and what is outside.

This adjective means “easily broken; fragile,” describing something that cannot withstand force or handling. It refers to weakness or brittleness rather than strength and is used as a descriptive word in the Greek LXX. This word occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Wisdom 15:13. The precise force of the description in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains something vulnerable to breaking or damage.

This proper name refers to the Euphrates, a river named throughout the Greek Old Testament and related writings. It is a geographical name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. The word appears 23 times in the Greek LXX corpus, from Genesis through 1 Maccabees. Its recurring use identifies the same well-known river in passages that mention lands, boundaries, journeys, or historical events, while the precise significance in any particular verse comes from that passage’s surrounding context.

Ephrath is a proper name, rendered “Ephrath” or “Efrath.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. The available references are 1 Chronicles 2:19 and 1 Chronicles 4:21. Its precise referent in each passage depends on the surrounding verse context, but the word itself functions as a specific name.

Eōbēs, also rendered Eovis, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular named entity. This form occurs once, in Joshua 15:59, so its exact referent and significance must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text rather than from the name alone. The available meaning is therefore the name itself, not a broader concept.

Zabouth, also rendered “Zavuth,” is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 4:5. Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is the person identified by that name, while the surrounding verse supplies any further information about him. The name itself does not carry an additional lexical definition in the available record.

This adjective means “tranquil,” describing a settled, undisturbed condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 66:2, so its recorded use is limited to that passage rather than spread across many texts. It presents calmness as a quality or condition, but the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there. Its central idea is quiet steadiness rather than agitation or turmoil.

Ēphad, also rendered Ifath, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name’s place in that genealogy cannot be explained further. Its normal function is simply to distinguish the individual bearing the name from others mentioned in the passage.

This noun refers to a dune or mound—an elevated heap or ridge of earth or sand. It names a physical feature rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament translation, it occurs once, in Baruch 5:7. The exact significance of the feature in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to something raised above the surrounding ground. Its meaning is concrete and descriptive: a natural or formed rise such as a sandy dune or earthen mound.

Idithōn, also rendered Ithithon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament, appearing eleven times across nine verses in 1 and 2 Chronicles. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not explain its etymology or the individual’s role. Its precise significance in any particular verse therefore comes from that passage’s surrounding context.

This proper name identifies the city called “Hierosolyma,” also rendered “Ierosolima.” It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 14 times, all in the Deuterocanonical writings, especially 2 Maccabees. The word appears in passages from 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each passage’s particular emphasis.

Iepheria, also rendered Ieferia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:25. The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whose name it is or what role that person has in the passage. Its meaning here is therefore best understood as the personal name Iepheria or Ieferia, with the immediate context supplying the person’s specific identity.

This Greek LXX word means “force,” referring to strength, power, or the ability to act effectively. As a noun, it names such power; as an adjective, it can describe something strong or forceful. It occurs 299 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, so it is used broadly for strength rather than only for physical might. Its precise emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Iōsaphat” or “Iosafat.” It functions as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 90 times across 77 verses, especially in Chronicles and Kings. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the personal name itself.

Kainan, also rendered Kenan, is a proper name belonging to a person in the Old Testament genealogy. It identifies the same named individual wherever it occurs rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears 13 times across 10 verses, chiefly in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding genealogy or list of names, but the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

This Greek LXX noun means “furnace,” referring to an enclosed structure or chamber used for intense heating. It is a concrete word for a place where heat is concentrated, rather than a description of the fire itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 9. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic meaning remains a furnace or heated chamber.

This verb means to feel shame—to experience an inward sense of disgrace or embarrassment. It describes a person’s emotional response rather than naming the shame itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:12. The reference identifies where the word appears, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular situation and force of that occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun refers to dissolving—the breaking apart, loosening, or ending of something. It can describe a process in which something once held together is brought to an end or reduced from its former condition. The related idea may apply to structures, arrangements, or established conditions, depending on the surrounding verse. This word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring but relatively limited use. Its central meaning remains the act or result of dissolution.

This noun means “downfall” or “calamity”—a disastrous collapse, ruin, or severe misfortune. It names the harmful event or condition itself rather than describing a person who causes it. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a serious reversal that brings ruin or distress.

This Greek LXX verb means to accuse someone—to charge a person with wrongdoing or present a complaint against them. It describes an act of alleging guilt, whether the accusation is justified or not; the surrounding passage determines that question. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Daniel and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on making an accusation against another person.

This verb means “put to sleep,” describing the act of causing someone to sleep. It focuses on what one person does to another rather than simply describing a state of sleeping. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across 11 verses, so it represents a recurring action word rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

This word means “scarlet,” referring to a vivid red color. It is an adjective, so it describes objects, materials, or clothing rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 43 times, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle, priestly garments, fabrics, and other valuable or striking items. Its use stretches from Genesis through Song of Songs, showing a recurring color term across different kinds of passages. The precise significance of scarlet in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “judge” or “decide.” It describes making a determination about a matter, person, or situation and expressing a judgment. The word is used broadly across the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, appearing 195 times, so its precise force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. It may refer to an authority making a ruling, or more generally to reaching a decision. This is an LXX Greek word and should be understood within that corpus.

This word means “talk,” referring to spoken words or conversation. As a noun in the Greek Septuagint, it identifies speech as something expressed or heard rather than describing an action itself. It occurs 22 times across the Septuagint, in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its use in passages from Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, and Daniel shows that it belongs to ordinary language for human or other spoken communication.

This word means “peel,” referring to the outer covering removed from something such as a plant or object. It is a noun, so it names that covering rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 30:37. The word’s basic sense is clear, while the precise significance of the object mentioned there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is a proper name rendered “Loud” or “Luth.” It identifies a named individual, people group, or place depending on the passage, but the available information does not establish which referent applies in each occurrence. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in Genesis 10:22 and once in Isaiah 66:19. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name alone.

Makeloth is a proper name, identifying a named place or location in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Greek text, both times in Numbers 33, at Numbers 33:25 and 33:26. Its precise significance beyond identifying this named location is not given by the available lexical information.

Maraia is a proper name, with Marea also given as a form of the name. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once, at Nehemiah 12:12. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, the name itself supports identifying a person, but not further claims about that person's role or significance.

This word means “me,” referring to the speaker or person receiving an action in a sentence. It is a pronoun, so it stands in place of a person’s name rather than describing a quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 1,577 times, showing that it is a common way to refer to oneself. Its exact emphasis—such as whether someone is being addressed, helped, blamed, or remembered—comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “bee,” the flying insect known for living and working in a hive. It is a noun, so it names the creature itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, sometimes in the singular and sometimes referring to bees as a group. Its appearances span several books, including Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. The ordinary meaning remains straightforward: a bee or bees, with the surrounding verse determining the particular comparison or setting.

This adjective describes someone who hates mankind—that is, a person characterized by hostility or aversion toward human beings. It can be rendered as “hating mankind” or “misanthropic,” with both phrases expressing the same central idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 11:4. The surrounding verse text is not included, so this cache explains the word’s normal meaning rather than its specific force in that passage.

Moloch, also rendered Molokh, is a proper name preserved as the name of a particular figure. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, each in a different verse: 2 Kings 23:10, Jeremiah 39:35, and Amos 5:26. The word itself identifies rather than describes, so its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context. The consistent rendering “Moloch” keeps this name distinct from ordinary descriptive words.

Mousi, also rendered Musi, is a personal name used for an individual or family line in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than as a general description or action word. This name appears eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, in passages from Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Its meaning is therefore chiefly its identification of a person or lineage, while the surrounding verse determines which bearer of the name is intended.

This word means “marrow,” the soft substance inside a bone. It is a noun naming a physical part of the body, so its basic sense is straightforward rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Genesis and twice in Job. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself consistently refers to marrow.

This word means “chick,” referring to a young bird. It is a noun used for a bird in its early stage of life, before it has fully matured. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times across 19 verses, including passages in Leviticus, Job, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic reference remains a young bird.

“Turn into weapons” is a verb describing the act of making something serve as weapons. It points to preparation or transformation rather than merely possessing a weapon. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs once, so its normal lexical sense is clear, while the precise force of its single use depends on the surrounding verse and passage. It should therefore be understood as an action word: to turn something into weapons.

This noun refers to “great deeds”—not merely ordinary actions, but notable works understood as impressive or significant. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Sirach, showing that it is a rare term within this corpus. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains deeds marked by greatness or remarkable accomplishment.

This word means “all-powerful”: it describes someone or something understood as having unlimited power. As an adjective, it adds this quality to the person or thing being described, rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in Wisdom. Its precise force in any one passage comes from the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains the description of power without limitation.

This Greek LXX verb means “neglect” or “slack,” describing the act of letting something go unattended, weakened, or unfulfilled. It can refer to failing to care for a duty or allowing something to become loose or ineffective. The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is established across more than one setting. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “twine around”: it describes the action of winding or wrapping something around another thing. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, across four Old Testament and three deuterocanonical verses. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This noun means “bitterness” or “bitter feeling”—an inward experience of resentment, sorrow, or emotional sharpness. It describes a person’s troubled inner state rather than an outward object or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 4:17. The surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of the word there, but its central meaning remains a deeply bitter or anguished feeling.

This adjective describes a person as a “fornicator” or “whoremonger”—someone identified by sexual unfaithfulness or prostitution. It functions as a characterizing term rather than naming an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:21. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that verse must be read from its context.

This Greek LXX verb means “go out for foraging.” It describes the action of leaving a place to search or gather provisions. As a verb, it focuses on the activity itself rather than naming a person, object, or place. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used in more than one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to “find rest with” someone or something. It describes settling into rest alongside another, rather than simply resting alone. As a verb, it expresses an action or experience of finding such rest. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in Wisdom 8:16. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is to find rest with another.

This adjective means “earlier,” describing someone or something that came, happened, or existed before another person or event. It marks a temporal comparison, pointing back to what preceded the present subject or situation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 43 times, so its basic use is broad but consistent: it identifies what is prior in time. The exact comparison becomes clear from the surrounding words in each passage.

Sauchaios, also rendered Safkheos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in Job: once in Job 2:11 and again in Job 42:17. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself gives no further lexical meaning beyond identifying the person called Sauchaios or Safkheos.

Semion is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:20. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the passage. Its meaning here is therefore the proper name Semion.

This noun means a mound: a raised heap or hill-like pile of earth or material. It names a physical feature rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 23:17. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the precise significance of the mound in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Sobochai, also rendered Sovokhe, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person. This name occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles: 11:29, 20:4, and 27:11. Because names identify individuals instead of expressing a general definition, its precise significance cannot be determined from the name alone. The spelling Sobochai follows the rendering used in the cited passages.

σοφῶς means “wisely”: it describes how an action is performed, with wisdom and sound judgment. As an adverb, it modifies an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in Isaiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains acting wisely rather than carelessly.

This verb means “defiled with”: it describes being made impure or stained through association with something defiling. As a verb, it expresses an action or condition rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Baruch 3:11. The word’s basic sense is therefore direct and focused: to be defiled through contact or connection with something regarded as impure. Its precise force in that verse is determined by the surrounding wording and passage.

This LXX Greek verb means being conscious or aware of something. It describes a person who recognizes, knows, or remains inwardly aware of a matter rather than being ignorant of it. The word appears 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, with uses spanning Leviticus, Job, Daniel, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is clear awareness or consciousness.

This verb means “draw together” or “draw up.” It describes an action of pulling things together or bringing them upward, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 27:3. Its exact force in that verse must come from the passage’s wording and context, but the central idea remains an active drawing or gathering movement rather than a state or quality. The word is therefore a verb describing what someone does: drawing together or drawing up.

This Greek noun means “savior”: a person who saves. It identifies one regarded as the source of salvation or rescue, whether spoken of in relation to God or to a human deliverer. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 31 times, so it is a recurring title or description rather than a rare term. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “honor” or “value”—to treat someone or something as worthy of respect, importance, or proper regard. It can describe honoring people, valuing something, or assigning it worth. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, it occurs 45 times, showing a broad use for esteem and valuation rather than a single narrow action. Its exact emphasis in a particular verse depends on what person or thing is being honored or valued there.

This noun refers to a “wounded one”—a person who has been injured. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 82 times, so it is used repeatedly for people marked by bodily injury rather than for an abstract condition. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains someone wounded.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “wheel,” referring to a round object that turns around an axle or supports movement. It can describe ordinary wheels used with carts or equipment, and it also appears in passages using wheels in crafted objects or vivid prophetic imagery. The word occurs 57 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, with especially frequent use in Ezekiel. Its basic sense remains consistent: a circular, turning structure used for movement or as part of a larger object.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “prevail over”: to overcome another person or force and gain the upper hand. It describes successful superiority or dominance rather than merely taking part in a struggle. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis, Joshua, and 2 Samuel. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its basic idea remains overcoming or proving stronger than what is opposed.

This word means “line of battle” or “battle-array,” describing an organized formation of fighting troops. As a noun, it refers not simply to combat but to soldiers arranged together for battle. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in 1 Maccabees, from 1 Maccabees 6:35 through 10:82. Its use therefore centers on military order and formation rather than a general idea of conflict.

Chabor, also rendered Khavor, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. Its role is to identify a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 5:26. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not identify more about the person, place, or thing it names.

Charmi, also rendered Kharmi, is a proper name used for a person or family line in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual concept; it identifies individuals within genealogical and historical records. The name occurs eight times across seven Old Testament verses, from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding names and statements in that passage.

This word means “dry land” or “land,” referring to ground rather than water. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings to identify an area of earth or country. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Isaiah and Hosea, and once in Wisdom. Its exact significance in any sentence comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains land or dry ground.

This noun means “greenness,” referring to the quality or appearance of being green. It describes green color or freshness rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalms 67:14. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition or appearance of being green. Scripture uses this word only in that single recorded occurrence within the Greek Old Testament corpus.

The word means “psalm,” a noun referring to a psalm. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 82 times, with 72 occurrences in Psalms. Its repeated use in the titles and headings of Psalms identifies the kind of sacred composition being presented, without by itself describing the subject or message of each individual psalm. The word also appears in 1 Samuel, Job, Lamentations, and 3 Maccabees, showing that its use is not limited to the book named Psalms.

Oronin is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a named person, place, or other entity in the biblical account. The name itself is rendered “Oronin,” and no broader descriptive meaning is given. It appears twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Joshua 10:10–11. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage rather than by the name alone.
